reply_text:
㊣ ("the need to verify compiled-correct rows per fix is low") Agreed. Fixes will no longer recheck rows that already compile correctly. A fix is accepted on three things:
- the target row's cold comparator result, before and after;
- a test that fails without the change and passes with it;
- the next stop it reaches, printed.

I've written this into the instructions every new packet starts with and into my wake checklist, and dropped the function-call recheck packet I proposed last turn.

㊟ (jobs already running) Two jobs already started include some correct rows as controls: codex-30's `bg-868` and codex-31's stop C matrix. I'll let them finish rather than cancel them partway. No new packet will ask for controls. I'll still read `AUDIT-20.md` once when lane 807 lands, because that's the only time the comparator has been run over the correct rows.

㊩ (the risk) One earlier fix, `0c2e4898`, did break the `term[_]` row, which was already correct, and only a control run caught it. If a correct row stops working later, it will show up when we next run it. Without the per-fix rechecks, we won't know which fix broke it.

previous_reply_acts.text: The audit already compares terms, not behaviour. Its cost is the cold compile: before the port can show its terms for a row, it has to compile everything that row depends on, starting from an empty cache. That took 5 to 20 minutes per row, so 20 rows across 4 lanes took about 75 minutes. Rechecking all correct rows after every fix would cost that each time. Your suggestion to go by function calls would cut most of it: record which parts of the port's compiler each row goes through, and recheck only the rows a fix touches.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: ("based on function calls rather than behaviour") Each audit lane runs the comparator: it captures the port's elaborated terms and compares them node by node with Lean's dump. No `#eval` behaviour checks run, and the comparison itself takes seconds. The time goes on the compile before it. The port compiles from source, so even `Lean.Syntax.isNone` first compiles parts of `Init`, `Array` and `Syntax`. Of the 20 lanes, 19 finished between 09:39 and 10:54.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text:
(cheaper rechecks) Two changes, in this order:
1. **Recheck only the rows a fix can affect.** On one cold run, record which functions in the port's compiler each correct row goes through (Python's tracer, once per row). When a fix changes some of those functions, recheck only the rows that went through them. Most fixes touch one elaborator path, such as structure instances or do-notation lifting, so most rows would be skipped. A safe default for a fix to shared code is to recheck everything. We'd also need a check that the recorded function list is complete. A planted change to a function must flag its rows.
2. **Run one cold compile for all rows together.** The rows share most of their dependencies, so one fresh compile in one process can capture terms for every correct row. That's still cold for deciding a merge, and it costs about one large compile instead of twenty. We first chose one cache per row so that rows couldn't contaminate each other through the cache. Within one fresh run, that worry doesn't apply.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (the warm cache) The proper fix is a warm cache we can trust: one that includes the compiler's own version in its key. Then a recheck would recompile only what the fix changed. We haven't found the cause of the warm-vs-cold difference yet, so cold stays the rule for decisions until we do.
